profile_narrative:
She's in her mid-thirties, hybrid job, somewhere on the city's edge where the houses back onto fields that should make for good dog walks but mostly don't anymore. She adopted a lurcher — two years old when she got him, already carrying whatever the first two years held — and she has been trying ever since. The diffuser that made the hallway smell odd and did nothing. The £14 wrap from Amazon that he wriggled out of in forty seconds. Two sessions with a behaviourist at £180 each, homework she did faithfully, no lasting change. She sets her alarm for 6am so they can walk before the neighbourhood wakes up, before someone else's dog comes around a corner and sends him flat to the pavement while strangers slow down to look.

Then a reel stopped her scrolling. A dog called Bramble, asleep through a thunderstorm. She watched it twice before she went looking for the page.

She does not buy quickly. She reads the about page. She checks the returns policy. She searches the product name plus 'rescue dog' in Facebook groups she already belongs to and trusts. The price makes her stop — she has done the mental arithmetic on everything she has already spent — but what breaks the hesitation is not a discount code. It is the handwritten note about introducing the coat slowly. It is someone writing as if they already knew her dog was the kind of dog that needs slow.

When it works, she folds the coat up the next morning with something between relief and disbelief. Then she opens her phone and tells the group, without being asked, that this one is actually different. People in those groups trust her. She has earned it the hard way.
demographics: Woman, mid-thirties, commuter belt on the edge of a UK city, hybrid office and home worker, rescue dog owner with a non-standard-shaped breed adopted as an adult. Shops online, receives UK mainland delivery.
situation: Has owned an anxious rescue dog for at least one full year. Has already spent meaningful money across multiple failed solutions — pheromone diffusers, calming sprays, a cheap pressure wrap from Amazon, at least one professional behaviourist session, possibly puppy classes that made things worse. The dog is not deteriorating but not improving either, and she has quietly begun reorganising her life around his limitations: pre-dawn walks to avoid triggers, dread that builds through October, weekends away she no longer tries to book.
trigger_events: A bad bonfire night or thunderstorm where the dog shook, panted, or couldn't settle no matter what she tried
A walk that ended with the dog flat on the pavement refusing to move while strangers stopped to stare
A vet visit that ended with a recommendation to increase anxiety medication she is already uneasy about
Watching a social video of a specific dog sleeping calmly through a trigger event that her own dog cannot cope with
objections: £58 feels hard to justify when a near-identical-looking wrap on Amazon is £14 — especially after already spending money on things that promised calm and didn't deliver it
Rescue dogs with lurcher, whippet, or staffie-cross builds are notoriously difficult to fit and she will not pay for something that won't stay on or sit right
She has a drawer full of products that didn't work; she needs a concrete reason this is different before she hands over her card details again
desires_surface: A well-fitting anxiety wrap that genuinely calms her rescue dog during fireworks, thunderstorms, and unpredictable loud noises
desires_deep: Her evenings back — watching television in October without one eye on the window, a weekend away she has stopped letting herself plan, and permission to stop quietly believing that she has somehow failed the dog she chose to take home
verbatims: First bonfire night in three years where Willow slept instead of shaking herself sick. I actually cried a bit folding the coat up the next morning. Worth every penny.

honestly didnt expect much, we've got a drawer full of 'calming' stuff that did nothing. The den bed is the first thing Ted has ever chosen to get into on his own. He takes himself off to it now when the bins get collected.
Ordered Tuesday, arrived Thursday with a handwritten note on how to introduce the coat slowly. Nobody does that anymore. Fits his weird whippet chest perfectly too.
exclusions: Someone who straps the coat on cold at a fireworks display expecting an instant fix, then returns it muddy with a one-star review when the dog was still stressed
Someone who believes a frightened dog is a badly behaved or disobedient dog that needs a firmer hand rather than support
